1st edition · 2019 · O'Reilly Media

Database Internals

Alex Petrov

Subtitled A Deep Dive into How Distributed Data Systems Work. The book explains what happens inside a database in two parts:

  • Part I, Storage Engines: how a single node lays out, indexes, caches, logs and recovers data. It covers B-Trees and their variants, file formats, buffer management, transactions and recovery, and log-structured storage.
  • Part II, Distributed Systems: how many nodes cooperate. It covers system models and impossibility results, failure detection, leader election, replication and consistency, anti-entropy and gossip, distributed transactions and consensus.

Each chapter ends with a summary and further reading, and the bibliography is extensive.

How the book fits together

The book's two parts build bottom-up. The Part I conclusion uses three properties, buffering, immutability and ordering, to describe the storage structures it covered (Figure I-1). It notes that mixing them is a trade-off: making one operation cheaper makes another more expensive (pp. 165–166). The Part II opener defines participants, links and clocks, and describes distributed algorithms as local steps plus message exchange for coordination, cooperation, dissemination and consensus (pp. 167–169). Chapter 8 then sets out the fallacies, failure models and impossibility results that the remaining chapters work within.

The arrows are the vault's reading of the chapters' dependencies; the parts and chapter order are the book's.

Some threads run through both parts:

  • Logs appear as the WAL (5), LSM-Trees (7), replicated logs (11) and consensus (14).
  • Ordering and time appear as logical clocks and consistency models (11), TrueTime in Spanner (13) and terms in Raft (14).
  • Quorums appear as tunable consistency (11), Paxos and Flexible Paxos (14), and PBFT's 3f + 1 (14).

Simulations

Interactive models of the mechanisms the book describes. They are embedded in the lessons too; implementations are the vault’s own.

  • Chapter 2B⁺-Tree splits and mergesInsert and delete keys in a B+-Tree with a chosen node capacity and watch splits promote separator keys, merges demote them, and the tree grow or shrink a level.
  • Chapter 3Slotted page: sorted pointers, unsorted cellsInsert and delete variable-size records in a slotted page: the cell-pointer array stays sorted by key while cells stay where they were written; freed space goes on an availability list filled by first fit or best fit, and defragmentation reclaims fragments.
  • Chapter 5ARIES: analysis, redo, undoRun a short workload with steal/no-force buffering and a fuzzy checkpoint, crash at any point, then step through ARIES analysis, redo and undo, including compensation log records that make recovery restartable.
  • Chapter 5Latch crabbing down a B-TreeDescend a B-Tree for a read, an insert or a delete with latch crabbing: latch the child, then release the ancestors if the child is safe. See which latches are held at each step and why a full or minimal child keeps the parent latched.
  • Chapter 5Page replacement: FIFO, LRU, CLOCK, LFUReplay a page-reference string through a buffer pool under FIFO, LRU, CLOCK and LFU, change the number of frames, and watch hits, misses, the clock hand and Bélády's anomaly.
  • Chapter 6Bw-Tree: delta chains and compare-and-swapPrepend delta records to logical pages through a mapping table, race two writers' compare-and-swap on the same page, watch read cost grow with chain length, and consolidate chains past a threshold.
  • Chapter 7LSM Trees: merge-iteration and compactionWrite, overwrite and delete keys in an LSM Tree, flush memtables to sorted tables, step through the book's merge-iteration example, and compare leveled and size-tiered compaction by tables per read, records rewritten and space used.
  • Chapter 8From fair-loss to perfect linksSend numbered messages over a link that loses, duplicates and reorders them, then add acknowledgments and retransmits, and finally sequence numbers with a reorder buffer and deduplication. Watch n_consecutive and n_processed.
  • Chapter 9φ-accrual vs a fixed deadlineFeed a monitored node heartbeats with adjustable jitter, pause or kill it, and watch the phi-accrual suspicion level climb against a threshold, next to a fixed-deadline detector on the same heartbeat stream.
  • Chapter 10Bully election, failover lists and split brainCrash the leader of six ranked processes, choose who notices, and step through Election, Alive and Elected messages of the bully algorithm; switch to next-in-line failover, or partition the cluster to see a split brain.
  • Chapter 11CRDTs: counters and sets that always mergePartition three replicas, increment, decrement, add and remove on each side, then heal the partition and watch G-Counter, PN-Counter and two-phase-set states merge to the same value regardless of merge order.
  • Chapter 11Quorums and witness replicasSet N, W and R, turn some replicas into witnesses, fail nodes, and issue writes and reads to see which succeed, whether a read is guaranteed to see the latest write, and when a witness is temporarily upgraded to hold data.
  • Chapter 11Vector clocks and causal deliveryBroadcast messages between three processes, deliver them in any order, and watch receivers buffer messages whose causal dependencies have not arrived yet. Compare two processes' vector clocks to see before, after or concurrent.
  • Chapter 12Gossip: spreading a rumour like an epidemicSeed one rumour in a cluster of 64 nodes, set the fanout and the interest-loss rule, and watch susceptible, infective and removed counts per round, total messages, redundancy, and nodes never reached.
  • Chapter 12Merkle trees: find the difference, not the dataDiverge two replicas of 16 keys, compare Merkle root hashes, and descend only into mismatching subtrees to find the ranges to stream. Change the leaf range size to trade tree size against repair precision.
  • Chapter 13Two-phase vs three-phase commit under failuresRun a commit round with a coordinator and three cohorts under two-phase or three-phase commit, crash the coordinator or partition a cohort, and compare the outcomes: 2PC blocks with uncertain cohorts, while 3PC finishes by timeout but can split into commit and abort.
  • Chapter 14Paxos, round by roundStep through single-decree Paxos with five acceptors and two proposers: a normal round, the book's three proposer-failure scenarios (Figures 14-4 to 14-6), and dueling proposers. Acceptors follow the real promise and accept rules, so the chosen value is computed, not scripted.

Key concepts

These ideas recur across chapters; each row lists the chapters that discuss them. The definitions are the vault's summaries of the book's explanations.

ConceptDefinitionChapters
B-TreeA balanced, high-fanout search tree whose nodes are disk pages. Lookups cost log_N(M) page reads, and inserts split overflowing nodes up to the root.2 · 4 · 6
Buffer pool (page cache)Pages cached in memory, with dirty pages flushed later. Eviction policies such as LRU, CLOCK and LFU decide what to drop.1 · 5
Write-ahead log (WAL)An append-only log persisted before data pages, used to redo or undo changes after a crash, as ARIES does.5 · 7
Buffering, immutability, orderingThe three properties the book uses to classify storage structures: whether writes are batched in memory, whether files are updated in place, and whether records are stored in key order.1 · 6 · 7
LSM-TreeBuffered writes in a memtable, flushed as immutable sorted tables and merged by compaction. Read, write and space amplification trade off against each other.7
Slotted pageA page layout with an array of pointers growing from one end and variable-size cells from the other, so records can be reordered without being moved.3 · 4
Isolation and concurrency controlRules for what concurrent transactions may see, enforced by locking (2PL), optimistic validation or multiversioning (MVCC).5 · 13
Failure detectorA component that suspects crashed processes, trading detection speed against accuracy. Heartbeats, φ-accrual and gossip are examples.8 · 9 · 14
Leader / split brainA single process that orders and coordinates work. Split brain is two leaders at once, which only majority-based protocols prevent.10 · 13 · 14
Consistency modelsGuarantees about the order and visibility of operations across replicas, from linearizability through causal consistency to eventual consistency.11 · 13
QuorumThe minimum number of nodes that must respond. Overlapping quorums (R + W > N, Q₁ + Q₂ > N) make sure some node sees both operations.11 · 14
Anti-entropyBackground repair of diverged replicas, using read repair, hinted handoff, Merkle trees or gossip.12
Atomic commitmentAll participants commit a transaction or none do: two-phase and three-phase commit, or commit built on consensus as in Spanner and Calvin.5 · 13
ConsensusCorrect processes agreeing on one proposed value despite failures. It is equivalent to atomic broadcast, and Paxos, Raft, ZAB and PBFT implement it.8 · 10 · 14
